There's also a Teen Titans Go episode about Pig Latin. Don't know what Pig Latin is? It's a language where you take all the consonants before the first vowel, move them to the end, and add '-ay' to the end. If the word begins with a vowel, you just add '-way' to the end. For example, "Waffles" becomes "Afflesway". I've been speaking Pig Latin fluently since the fourth grade, so it surprised me when I saw the episode for the first time. I speak Pig Latin with my sister sometimes. It's pretty fun. I like speaking it in public so that everyone around us gets confused. That's never actually happened before, but if it ever does, 'twill be pretty funny. By the way, "'twill" is a word I invented recently, and it's a contraction of "it will". I really hope it gains popularity in the near future, because "'twill" is WAY more fun than saying "it'll". "It'll" is too boring. Nobody likes boring.

eral different varieties of black hole systems. Also discussed are several different
criteria for explaining why these systems appear the way they do to observers and
for unifying them with other types of black hole system. Ultimately, we shall see
that all black hole systems (including the small ones in our own Galaxy) are funda-

it is rotating, how fast it consumes fuel, the angle at which we view it (relative to the
hole’s spin axis), and the nature of the environment in which the black hole resides.
There are traditionally three types of black hole systems: active galactic nuclei
(AGN, which includes quasars, radio and Seyfert galaxies, and a host of other ob-
jects), binary X-ray sources (now called “microquasars”), and the recently recog-
nized “intermediate mass” black holes (IMBH, with masses of one hundred to ten
thousand solar masses). In order to unify the terminology, I sometimes will refer to
AGN as “macroquasars” (large ones), IMBH as “miniquasars” (small ones), and bi-
nary X-ray sources as “microquasars” (tiny ones). This is a further evolution of the
word quasar (originally short for “quasi-stellar radio source”), which is already now
used to describe even radio-quiet AGN, and a likely direction for the terminology
to take as we learn more about the similarities among the structure and behavior of
these systems. For the original objects identified as quasi-stellar radio sources, we
will use the terms QSRs or RLQs (for radio-loud quasars).1

of doubly-ionized oxygen. Type 2 Seyfert galaxies (like NGC 1068) have permitted
lines with the same, rather narrow width of the forbidden lines (500–1000 km s−1).
Here, the word “permitted” really means that the atoms emitting these lines can
do so very quickly, before another process (such as a collision with another atom)
changes its excited atomic state. Forbidden transitions have a lower probability of
happening than permitted transitions; so atoms that emit forbidden lines generally
do so only if they are in a low-density environment with a long time between colli-
sions with other atoms.
